summary: Discusses considerations and methods for moving an Autonomous System (AS) to a new number while keeping BGPsec working and secure. It updates RFC 8205.

eli5.summary: When a company changes its name, it needs a way for the old signature to still be trusted. This explains how for BGPsec.

subtitle: How a router can keep BGPsec paths valid while an old AS number is being folded into a new one.

tldr.problem: AS migration deliberately rewrites the AS path, which is exactly what BGPsec is built to detect, and customers cannot be asked to change their configuration.
tldr.mechanism: The migrating PE router holds keys for both the old and new AS number and signs each update twice, linking the two with a signature that carries pCount=0 so the path length does not grow.
tldr.outcome: BGPsec can support AS migration without lengthening the path or reconfiguring the customer, at the cost of signing in iBGP and keeping the old AS key valid until migration ends.

today: RFC 8206 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2017. It updates RFC 8205, and the unit metadata shows no RFC has obsoleted or updated it.

sections.title: The Problem: Migrating an AS Under BGPsec
sections.content:
RFC 7705 (RFC 7705) describes how a provider can move routers from one Autonomous System Number (ASN) into another by manipulating the AS_PATH attribute. RFC 8205 defines BGPsec, which is explicitly designed to protect against changes in the AS_PATH, whether by choice, misconfiguration or malicious intent. The two goals collide, and this document, which updates RFC 8205, shows how BGPsec can support the migration tool without creating an unacceptable security risk.

The scenario is a provider merging two or more ASes so that one subsumes the others. BGP confederations are not enabled between them. Instead, a migrating Provider Edge (PE) router masquerades as the old ASN on its PE-CE eBGP session, manipulates the AS_PATH, or both. This differs from a BGPsec confederation: eBGP peers may not be peering with the correct ASN, and the signatures are for a public ASN, so nobody would strip them.

The examples use AS64510 being subsumed by AS64500, with AS64496 and 64499 as customer networks, taken from the documentation ASN range.
sections.eli5: Imagine a letter that must be stamped by every post office it passes. If one office changes its name halfway, the stamps still need to make sense.

sections.title: Why Migrations Last Long
sections.content:
The RFC notes that providers rarely stop after one merger, acquisition or divestiture, so they accumulate legacy ASNs. Because the migration methods are transparent to customers and need no coordination, no customer has an incentive to finish moving from the old ASN to the new one, and the transition can be protracted.

The working group considered the operational complexity and hardware scaling issues of keeping several legacy ASN keys on routers throughout the combined network. Saying "don't do this" would be of limited use, so the solution tries to minimize added complexity during a transition that is expected to be long. Enterprises migrate between ASNs with the same functionality, so the document is not only for service providers.
sections.eli5: Nobody is in a hurry to update their address book when a friend moves, so the old and new addresses both stay in use for a long time.

sections.title: Origin Validation, Path Validation and Requirements
sections.content:
Origin validation (RFC 6480) needs no change. For each Route Origination Authorization (ROA) that authorizes the old ASN to originate a prefix, a new ROA MUST also be created that authorizes the replacing ASN for the same prefix. Multiple ROAs of this kind are allowed, and they may exist side by side until every router originating from the old ASN has migrated.

Path validation is harder. Outbound (PE to CE), a PE moved to the new ASN signs with the new ASN, but BGPsec gives no guidance on whether the signed ASN must match the configured remote AS, and RFC 4271 lists that match only as an optional check. Inbound (CE to PE), the CE still signs toward the old ASN and the PE cannot alter earlier signatures, while leaving the old ASN in the path would lengthen it, which RFC 7705 calls unacceptable.

Any solution must meet these requirements:

  • MUST support migration for inbound and outbound announcements without reducing BGPsec protection.
  • MUST NOT require reconfiguration on the remote eBGP neighbor (CE).
  • SHOULD NOT require network-wide configuration changes.
  • MUST NOT lengthen the AS path.
  • MUST operate within existing trust boundaries, for example by not expecting a remote side to accept pCount=0 from an untrusted neighbor.
sections.eli5: The fix must not make the customer do anything, must not make the route look longer, and must not ask strangers to trust a trick they have not agreed to.

sections.title: The Solution: Sign Twice with pCount=0
sections.content:
BGPsec already has a way to hide an ASN: a pCount of 0 in a Secure_Path segment (Section 4.2 of RFC 8205). Simply keeping the old key on the PE and signing toward the CE with pCount=0 would pass pCount=0 between different administrative and trust domains, which could be a significant attack vector, and no customer coordination can be assumed.

A better idea comes from the inbound direction. Both ASNs are in the same administrative domain, so a signature from the old ASN forward-signed to the new ASN with pCount=0 stays inside a trust boundary. Applying this on all routes between the two ASNs could cause routing loops, so it belongs on the local PE that still has eBGP sessions with peers expecting the old ASN.

The PE acts as if it exists in both ASNs. Each update received from or sent to an eBGP neighbor still using the old ASN is signed twice: once with the ASN to be hidden and once with the ASN that stays visible. This is as if an internal hop crossed an eBGP session between the two ASNs using pCount=0, without the cost of a real session. Because the PE holds valid keys for both ASNs, the resulting path remains secured.

BGPsec neighbors exchange the Secure_Path, not the AS_PATH. When a BGPsec speaker talks to a non-BGPsec neighbor and rebuilds an AS_PATH, ASNs with pCount=0 do not appear at all. The document does not change that behavior.
sections.eli5: The router wears two name tags, the old one and the new one, and stamps the letter with both. The old tag is marked 'do not count', so the route does not look any longer.

sections.title: Outbound, Inbound and Other Rules
sections.content:
Outbound (PE to CE). For an eBGP neighbor configured with AS-migration mechanisms, the PE MUST generate valid BGPsec signatures for both configured ASNs. It MUST sign from the new (global) ASN to the old (local) ASN with pCount=0, and then MUST sign from the old ASN to the target eBGP ASN with pCount=1 as normal.

Inbound (CE to PE). The PE MUST generate a signature from the old (local) ASN forward-signing to the new (global) ASN with pCount=0. A second signature from the new ASN is not needed because the ASBR creates it when it signs toward its eBGP peers. Signing in iBGP is a change from normal behavior, for this migration case only.

Other considerations. BGPsec-capable routers receiving updates from iBGP neighbors MUST accept properly formed BGPsec attributes, including pCount=0 on a previous signature, and BGPsec-capable route reflectors MUST reflect these updates transparently to BGPsec-capable clients. The PE MUST hold valid keys for both ASNs, and the old ASN's key MUST stay valid until all eBGP sessions are migrated. Downstream neighbors see a valid path because they trust that the upstream accepted pCount=0 by explicit configuration, based on the trust relationship between old and new ASN. When RFC 7705 techniques make an iBGP session between different global ASNs, the same procedure applies, except the migrating router acts as the boundary between old and new ASN and MUST sign from old ASN to new with pCount=0.
sections.eli5: Going out, the router signs as the new name and then as the old name. Coming in, it signs as the old name pointing to the new one. Both name tags have to stay valid until the last customer has moved.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The example shows PE-1 being migrated from AS64510 into AS64500, with CE-1 in AS64496, CE-2 in AS64499 and an external peer AS64505. Before the merger, a route from CE-2 reaches CE-1 with Secure_Path (64510, 64500, 64499) and a path length of 3.

Outbound, after migration, PE-1 passes the route to CE-1 with Secure_Path (64510, 64500 (pCount=0), 64499). The equivalent AS_PATH is (64510, 64499) and the length is 2, not 3. PE-1 adds the segment signed as AS64500 and accepts it with pCount=0 acting as AS64510, as it would from an eBGP peer.

Inbound, a route from CE-1 arrives signed toward AS64510. PE-1 adds a signature as AS64510 toward AS64500 with pCount=0, so the Secure_Path is (64510 (pCount=0), 64496) and the length is 1, not 2. After PE-2 and the ASBR sign toward AS64505 or CE-2, the Secure_Path is (64500, 64510 (pCount=0), 64496), with an equivalent AS_PATH of (64500, 64496) and a length of 2, not 3.
sections.eli5: The example follows one letter in and out of the router and counts the stamps. The stamp from the old name is marked 'do not count', so the letter's trip looks the same length as it should.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The migration process rewrites the AS path so it differs from the path the route really took, which is exactly what BGPsec exists to prevent. BGPsec MUST be able to handle this legitimate use without opening a vulnerability in the RPKI route security infrastructure.

The RFC considers the solution reasonably secure against a malicious actor because both signatures must be made as though forward-signed between two eBGP neighbors. That requires valid keys for both the migrated and the subsumed ASN on the router. If an AS's keys are compromised, or zero-length keys are permitted, an AS_PATH shortening attack may become possible, but these are described as existing BGPsec risks. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A thief would need both name tags and both secret stamps to fake this, and having those would already be a problem for the old system too.
